ServiceNow unpacks the Fortune AIQ list, where the widest gap between AI leaders and laggards is training for humans
Diana David, ServiceNow director of futures · Fortune · Rebecca Greenfield—Fortune
Diana David calls herself a "forward-deployed futurist." She says CEOs kept asking for "forward-deployed" employees, "people to be out on the edge, to bring us back the insights about what is actually happening in AI in our companies."
What she is finding is that the companies pulling ahead on AI are not distinguished mainly by their technology. At the Fortune AIQ Summit on Thursday, David, who also serves as ServiceNow's director of futures, said the widest gaps between the leaders and everyone else are about people.
"Talent investment. That was the biggest gap," David told moderator Jeremy Kahn, Fortune's AI editor. In ServiceNow's Enterprise AI Maturity Index, 57% of "pacesetters" invest in ongoing AI upskilling, versus 4% of other organizations. By the report's figures, the single widest gap is in attracting, hiring, and retaining AI talent: 68% vs. 10%.
"It's really operational discipline, right?" David said. "It's not just technology—operational discipline and transformation."
Pacesetters are the roughly 21% of surveyed organizations that scored above 60 on the 100-point index, averaging 74 against 45 for the rest. Their edge extends beyond talent. By David's account, 64% are on a path to unified data, versus 14%. And around 57% have "a clear, strong AI vision," versus 21%.
Then there are the autonomous workflows. About 59% of companies surveyed are past the pilot phase, David said. "Only 9% are doing agentic, autonomous, multistep workflows that are not checked by human beings at every step." Among pacesetters the share is 36%, against 2% of others. These workflows are "not just one little point of sale," she said.
That distinction drives what David called her "pet peeve": "AI adoption for everyone."
"I get it, because it's a great CEO story," she said. "95% of everybody has X, Y, Z. But it is not translating into productivity, and it's often not with training, and that doesn't equal maturity."
Kahn had set up the problem. Many companies gave employees AI tools and "let a thousand flowers bloom," he said. Then they decided it was too expensive, with no productivity gain. Now they are narrowing to specific use cases. Kahn also pointed to companies that dropped agents into existing workflows, or swapped an employee for one.
David said the answer starts higher up. "I think it starts with leadership," she said. "Growth mindset, an idea, and a vision for change of what the company can become, followed with specific training around AI and specific functions."
She urged executives to think "almost in a day zero mentality" about what process would be designed from scratch. The alternative, she said, is to "sprinkle AI on something, probably a very old or broken process, to make it go even faster. That's just not solving the problem faster."
Kahn pressed on a worry he said executives voice: The technology moves so fast that a redesigned process may be obsolete next year. David said she hears that, too. Her answer was to have a vision, align the data, choose workflows, assign ownership, and "iterate … I don't think that any company is going to succeed by doing some kind of top-down plan where one person or one strategy team is redesigning everything immediately," she said.
She pointed to ServiceNow's AI Control Tower as one way to see across the organization. "You have to have transparency," she said. "Having the visibility from across the organization and a very strong foundation allows you to be flexible."
Most companies are behind on the human side. According to the report, 59% of organizations lack long-term HR plans for AI, and 42% of employees say they aren't getting enough AI training. The report puts pacesetters' average ROI at 160%.
The leaders are not confined to tech. David said technology companies took about one in five spots on Fortune's AIQ 75, followed by financial services. Construction and engineering took six, and food and health care five each.
"It is everything, everywhere, all at once," David said.
The index itself has been volatile. "In 2024 we started this, and we thought, 'It's just going to go up and up and up,'" David said. Then the average score fell from 44 to 35. Kahn noted the drop came "several years into the generative AI boom." David said the cause was that "the noise was out there, AI was everywhere, but it hadn't really filtered into company value." Scores rebounded to 51 this year.
"I can't promise you that there won't be another dip next year," she said.
She added that ServiceNow plans to add agentic AI to the AIQ next year, and the measure will turn on "what are we deploying and where," and whether companies are "realizing actual commercial value." That, she said, "is what I think true maturity for business is going to mean, versus everybody has, you know, AI in their pocket."
For this story, Fortune journalists used generative AI as a research tool. An editor verified the accuracy of the information before publishing.

Enterprise software is leading a rebound across technology stocks, and shares of ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW | NOW Price Prediction) sit at the front of the group. ServiceNow stock is up 4% to $139.73, moving in step with the closest names in application software. Gains are spread across several major application vendors at once, a sign of broad sector participation.
Also, shares of Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU) are up 4% to $285.50, matching the gain in ServiceNow stock. Meanwhile, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) shares are climbing 3% to $246.49, a slightly smaller gain pointed the same way. Workday (NASDAQ:WDAY) rounds out the enterprise software cluster, adding another large application vendor exposed to the same artificial intelligence (AI) debate.
Notably, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is up 1% to $107.95. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is up 0.5% to $743.20, a smaller advance for large-cap technology. Software’s lead over that broader benchmark marks this as a group bid concentrated in application vendors.
ServiceNow stock’s rally tracks a broad bid across enterprise software. The software sector fund is beating large-cap technology, and the two closest peers, Intuit and Adobe, are moving the same direction by similar amounts. That combination points to sector repair across the group, and ServiceNow stock is benefiting as money flows back into application software, since broad buying of that kind tends to lift the strongest operators and the weakest ones alike.
Workday belongs to the enterprise software cluster and faces the same questions about how AI changes application spending. Alongside ServiceNow, Intuit, and Adobe, Workday gives the group coverage of workflow, financial, creative, and human resources software, so the rebound reaches well beyond one product category. That breadth makes the enterprise cluster a cleaner read on sector sentiment than any single stock.
Disclosed AI Revenue Separates ServiceNow
Inside the group, ServiceNow carries a distinguishing fact: its AI products are already producing disclosed revenue. In the most recently reported quarter, ServiceNow stated that annual contract value from its AI products exceeded $1 billion. That figure speaks to the first argument around the company, which is whether AI products convert into reported sales.
ServiceNow also reported a renewal rate of 98% in that quarter, a sign the subscription base is holding while the market debates whether generative AI replaces software-as-a-service applications. Together, the two disclosures give ServiceNow stock stronger fundamental basis than a sector bounce supplies on its own.
For ServiceNow, a clear signal is whether the IGV fund keeps its lead over the broader technology benchmark, and traders can watch for whether that spread holds because it defines the rally lifting ServiceNow, Intuit, and Adobe shares. Any closing of that gap would suggest the software bid is fading into a more dull technology tone.
Traders should watch Intuit and Adobe shares. If they stop moving in step with ServiceNow stock, that split would hurt the sector-repair reading. A strong next quarterly update from ServiceNow could confirm that AI contract value keeps converting into reported revenue.
ServiceNow pairs disclosed AI traction with a 98% renewal rate, which reinforces the case for upside, while the displacement debate supports caution. Those holding the stock should size their positions carefully given that a single rally for software leaves that debate unresolved.

As artificial intelligence continues to transform enterprise software, investors are choosing between the steady expansion of ServiceNow (NOW -2.45%) and the explosive growth of Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%). This comparison explores which stock is the better buy.
ServiceNow specializes in automating business workflows for massive organizations, whereas Palantir provides deep-data analytics and decision-making platforms. While both are leaders in artificial intelligence, they target different operational needs and trade at very different prices. Understanding their financial health and risk profiles is essential for deciding which to add to your 2026 portfolio.
In its latest annual report, ServiceNow provides an AI platform designed to automate work across IT, HR, and customer service departments for roughly 8,400 customers. The company has a massive footprint among large enterprises, with 86% of the Fortune 500 utilizing its services. It maintains strategic alliances with several prominent tech stocks, including Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) and Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%).
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $13.3 billion, which is a growth of approximately 20.9% compared to the previous year. This steady expansion resulted in a net income of close to $1.7 billion for the fiscal year. The company's focus on high-value corporate clients has allowed it to maintain a consistent net margin of roughly 13.2%.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x, which means the company uses very little total debt relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio, a measure of whether a business can pay its short-term debts with short-term assets, is nearly 1.0x while free cash flow reached nearly $4.6 billion for FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 35.9% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
According to its latest annual report, Palantir builds software platforms like Gotham and Foundry for AI-driven decision-making and operational workflows. The company serves a mix of government and commercial enterprises, including long-term contracts with the U.S. Army and other national security entities. Key partners helping expand its reach include Nebius Group (NBIS +4.53%) and Fujitsu (FJTSF +0.97%).
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $4.5 billion, which represents growth of approximately 56.2% compared to the previous year. This rapid expansion helped the company achieve net income of close to $1.6 billion. This is a significant increase from the net income reported in 2024, showing the business is successfully scaling its operations and achieving a net margin of roughly 36.3%.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.0x, indicating a very clean balance sheet with virtually no debt. The current ratio is roughly 7.1x, and free cash flow for FY 2025 reached close to $2.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 32% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
ServiceNow faces intense competition from established software vendors such as Microsoft, Oracle (ORCL +3.06%), SAP (SAP -1.05%), Salesforce (CRM -0.84%), and Workday (WDAY -0.33%). Regulatory risks involve complex data privacy laws and increasing scrutiny of government procurement processes and potential bid protests. Technology risks include the potential for AI integrations to result in unreliable or biased outputs, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and the dependency on third-party public cloud providers for infrastructure scalability.
Palantir is subject to intense competition from large enterprise software firms, defense contractors, and system integrators. A significant risk involves its reliance on a limited number of customers, where the loss or non-renewal of large contracts could materially impact financial results. It also depends on third-party cloud infrastructure provided by Amazon (AMZN +1.32%) and Microsoft. Additionally, the company faces potential cybersecurity breaches involving sensitive client data and public scrutiny regarding its work with government entities.
Palantir commands a much higher Forward P/E and P/S ratio, which measures market cap against sales over the past twelve months, than ServiceNow.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with Palantir. Its Q2 results were among the most extraordinary posted by any software company in recent memory. Revenue nearly doubled year over year, and U.S. commercial revenue grew so fast that even Palantir's CEO described the quarter as otherworldly. And the momentum looks set to continue, with the company yet again raising its full-year outlook. Palantir is profitable, generating substantial free cash flow, and somehow still accelerating.
ServiceNow is a winner in its own right. Its workflow platform is so deeply embedded in how large enterprises run their operations that replacing it is rarely worth the disruption. Subscription revenue is growing at a consistent double-digit rate, enterprises keep signing larger and longer deals, and the business generates substantial free cash flow. For investors who prioritize durability and predictability, it is a strong long-term hold.
But Palantir's combination of hypergrowth and profitability is rare at any scale. The valuation demands consistent execution, but so far the results keep justifying the confidence.

ServiceNow stock (ISIN US81762P1021) closed at USD 135.47 on Nasdaq on September 18, 2026, down 2.17 percent from the prior session, even as expectations for earnings and revenue growth remain robust for the coming quarters.
According to finance portal data for ServiceNow, Inc. (ticker NOW), the shares last traded at USD 135.47 at the close on September 18, 2026, representing a 2.17 percent decline on the day and reflecting a period of heightened volatility around large-cap software names.
Per Nasdaq-linked quote information, the after-hours indication on September 18, 2026 was USD 136.01, modestly above the official close and signaling cautious buying interest following the intraday drop.
On September 19, 2026, an update from a trading app showed that ServiceNow shares were valued at USD 136.04, with the stock trading between an intraday low of USD 135.07 and a high of USD 139.94 on that date, and a volume of 19.25 million shares compared with an average daily volume of 13.36 million shares, underlining above-normal activity as investors reassessed the sector.
The same snapshot put ServiceNow’s market capitalization at USD 139.78 billion as of September 19, 2026, a level that highlights the company’s position among the largest business software providers globally.
In its most recent reported quarter, ending in the second quarter of 2026, ServiceNow achieved revenue growth in the mid-20 percent range year over year, confirming that demand for its workflow and digital transformation platform remains strong across enterprise customers.
According to a recent analysis that summarized the July 22, 2026 earnings release, ServiceNow reported quarterly earnings per share of USD 0.90 for that second-quarter period, beating the consensus estimate by USD 0.04 and delivering revenue growth of 24.0 percent compared with the same quarter a year earlier, a combination that reinforced the company’s premium valuation.
The same overview noted that the company’s management raised its subscription revenue guidance for fiscal year 2026 to a range of USD 15.755 billion to USD 15.770 billion, with third-quarter 2026 subscription revenue projected between USD 3.975 billion and USD 3.980 billion and an operating margin target of 31 percent, signaling confidence in continued scalable growth.
ServiceNow has also highlighted the traction of its artificial intelligence offerings, with one data provider pointing out that its AI products crossed USD 1.0 billion in annual contract value in the second quarter of 2026, adding a new layer of recurring revenue on top of the core platform business.
Looking ahead to the next set of results, a recent article from an equity research-focused outlet reported that analysts expect ServiceNow to post earnings per share of USD 1.03 for the upcoming quarter, up 7.29 percent from the prior-year quarter, and revenue of USD 4.1 billion, up 20.27 percent year over year, keeping the company firmly in the high-growth camp within enterprise software.
For the full year 2026, the same consensus snapshot indicated projected earnings of USD 4.06 per share and revenue of USD 16.2 billion, which would represent increases of 15.67 percent and 22.02 percent, respectively, versus the previous fiscal year, underscoring that the recent share-price pullback is occurring against the backdrop of double-digit fundamental growth.
Analyst ratings and sentiment around ServiceNow stock
As one MarketBeat.com overview on September 19, 2026 detailed, ServiceNow currently carries a consensus rating of Moderate Buy among covering analysts, based on one Strong Buy rating, thirty-six Buy ratings, three Hold ratings and two Sell ratings on the stock.
The same aggregated data set places the consensus 12-month price target for ServiceNow at USD 145.71, implying upside of roughly 7 percent from the September 18, 2026 closing level of USD 135.47 and reflecting continued confidence in the company’s ability to execute on its subscription and AI-led growth strategy.
Within that dispersion of views, individual price targets range from about USD 72 on the bearish end, associated with an Underperform stance, to USD 160 on the bullish end with an Outperform rating, highlighting that while most analysts see further gains, there is a cohort that questions the sustainability of the valuation if macro or spending conditions worsen.
In addition, recent institutional activity has remained supportive, with one report on September 19, 2026 noting that Nykredit A S established new holdings in ServiceNow, signaling ongoing interest from professional investors who are willing to look through short-term price volatility to the company’s longer-term transformation thesis.
ServiceNow’s share-price swings are not occurring in isolation but are tightly linked to sentiment in the broader cloud and software sector, where concerns about artificial intelligence monetization, interest-rate trajectories and enterprise budget cycles have periodically weighed on valuations.
An earlier sector-wide review described how nervousness around artificial intelligence themes and upcoming inflation data led to a retreat across software names, with ServiceNow falling about 5 percent alongside peers such as Salesforce and Intuit before rebounding in subsequent sessions on the back of stronger-than-expected AI-related results from another data-platform company.
Those whipsaw moves translated into seven-day declines that outpaced what the fundamental news flow alone might justify, and a 30-day performance pattern in which ServiceNow shares remained modestly positive overall, illustrating how sentiment-driven volatility can temporarily obscure a fundamentally improving earnings and revenue picture.
For investors, the key risk factor remains the possibility that enterprises delay or trim digital transformation and AI-related spending if macroeconomic uncertainty rises, which could put pressure on the ambitious revenue and margin guidance that currently underpins the consensus price targets.
On the other hand, the company’s growing base of subscription revenue, its expanding AI contract value and its track record of year-over-year revenue growth in the 20 percent-plus range offer mitigating factors against these risks, as even a modest deceleration would still leave ServiceNow among the faster-growing large-cap software names.
ServiceNow stock thus currently trades in the mid-USD 130s, below the roughly USD 145.71 analyst consensus target and within a volatile range that recently saw intraday levels between USD 135.07 and USD 139.94 on September 19, 2026, giving investors a window of roughly 3.6 percent between the short-term low and high in the most recent session.
The next major fundamental checkpoint for the shares is the upcoming third-quarter 2026 earnings report, scheduled for October 28, 2026 according to a recent earnings calendar summary, when management will update its guidance and provide new data points on subscription revenue, operating margins and AI product traction that are likely to influence whether the stock moves closer to or further away from the current consensus price target.

ServiceNow’s AI-Powered Flow Service Desk Aims To Open Midmarket Opportunities
ServiceNow is expanding beyond large enterprises with Flow by ServiceNow, an AI-powered conversational IT service desk designed for rapid deployment in midmarket businesses, opening new customer opportunities for channel partners while supporting Slack, Teams, and stand-alone or integrated platform deployments.
ServiceNow Thursday introduced a new AI-powered service desk offering, and in the process made its first serious foray into expanding its business beyond the large enterprises typically it serves.
The new Flow by ServiceNow offering aims to bring the company’s IT service management (ITSM) technology to what is for the company its first AI-native offering aimed at the “Fortune 500,000,” as originally hinted at in July by Chairman and CEO Bill McDermott during ServiceNow’s second fiscal quarter 2026 quarterly financial report.
The Fortune 500,000 refers to the midrange and commercial market.
[Related: ServiceNow To Target ‘Fortune 500,000’ Customers With New AI-Native Play]
Flow by ServiceNow is a new stand-alone conversational AI service desk that can help resolve employees’ issues and requests in new ways in the channels they operate and already use, said Jeff Hausman, the company’s executive vice president and general manager for technology workflow products.
“This allows customers to more quickly build and deliver solutions so they don’t repeat and manually have to address problems over and over again,” Hausman told CRN.
Flow by ServiceNow is a very quick and easily deployed technology that can be set up and running within minutes or hours, Hausman said.
“As an example, many customers are saying to us, ‘The way I want to operate is, I want to have a Teams or Slack chat channel, and I want all of my employees to coexist in that channel and be able to ask questions and get the answers in one common place,’” he said. “The Flow experience allows you to do that.”
Flow by ServiceNow targets existing ServiceNow enterprise customers as well as midsize and smaller business users, Hausman said.
For existing customers, it works in multiple sites and locations away from a company’s core or central operations, he said.
“You might want to offer them this new way of working with an easy-to-deploy [offering to] run their service desk,” he said. “Everything you do in that service desk can be, if you’re an existing customer, bidirectionally synced back to the core so you still have all the guardrails of tracking and understanding securely what was done, how it was done, how it was responded, the reporting aspects of all the incidents or issues, and changes that were made.”
Net-new customers can stand up from scratch a new service desk experience that is independent of and does not require the core platform, Hausman said.
Michael Park, ServiceNow’s senior vice president of global partnerships and channels, told CRN via email that Flow will open market segments ServiceNow has never been able to reach before.
“That’s real opportunity for our partner ecosystem, especially those operating across the commercial and midmarket segments,” Park said. “A company running IT out of Slack and spreadsheets isn’t a ServiceNow prospect today; Flow makes them one. These partners get a brand-new way to acquire customers and a low-friction entry point that creates immediate customer value and opens the door to broader platform adoption over time.”
Pricing is consumption-based based on the usage of ServiceNow’s Now Assist packs or Now Assist credits, Hausman said. As a result, every existing customer already using the company’s Now Assist GenAI-powered applications immediately have the means to start using Flow, he said.
Hausman said ServiceNow is still working on the specifics of how to charge new customers, which include both larger and smaller companies, that may not deploy Now Assist.
Flow by ServiceNow is already being taken by channel partners to new and existing customers, Hausman said. All its channel partners already know the application, he said.
“The good news is that we do have a number of existing partners who actually touch different organizations than our traditional kind of larger customers,” he said. “So we’re working with a number of them, but we’re certainly open to working with, and we will be talking to, potentially other partners that might make sense.”
ServiceNow is already educating partners on Flow by ServiceNow, and those already certified with the company’s ITSM or related technologies will be offered an extension to their current certifications, he said.
Solution providers that currently do not work with ServiceNow will not require ServiceNow expertise or capabilities to work with Flow by ServiceNow, Hausman said.
“That expertise is nice to have in case you want to tie it to the wider ServiceNow technology, but if you’re running it completely stand-alone, it’s not required,” he said.
Flow by ServiceNow initially targets businesses’ service desk requirements for internal employees, but that could be expanded to supporting external users in the future, Hausman said.
“I think we’ll have to see where it evolves,” he said. “The very first design principle and where we’ve been focused on is helping customers manage their internal communications and internal responses. But certainly, we could see this potentially growing. And honestly, we will follow where customers’ needs evolve. They’ve been asking us and focusing us on managing all their internal requests. But there’s certainly no reason why Flow couldn’t be extended in the future.”
Flow by ServiceNow is slated to be available for existing customers in North America starting Oct. 6, and then for all existing and new customers worldwide later in the fourth calendar quarter, Hausman said.
Flow by ServiceNow is a good play for the midmarket, said Ryan Crosby, vice president of sales for the intelligent ops practice at Ahead, a Chicago-based solution provider and ServiceNow channel partner ranked No. 24 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500.
“There’s a lot going on right now in the market, specifically in the midmarket,” Crosby told CRN. ... It’s a more simplistic way of being able to deploy AI-native service desks for customers’ businesses. So I like the fact that they’re moving in this direction. I like the fact that it’s getting away from ServiceNow’s traditional seat-based license model. I honestly think it’ll be a play for both the enterprise and the commercial and midmarket space.”
Crosby said Flow by ServiceNow will be a faster way for customers to deploy AI in their businesses.
“I think it’s more for a lot of the edge use cases,” he said. “For example, when a customer wants an alternative for Teams or Slack. Partners can make this a really good beachhead for offering service desks to some of their customers’ edge use cases that they haven’t been able to historically go after.”
While Ahead has hitched its business to ServiceNow and the enterprise, Crosby said his company has the capacity to reach a wider range of customers with Flow by ServiceNow.
“We’ve already started doing that,” he said. “We’ve already made a companywide investment in the midmarket,” he said. “We started that investment a little over a year ago. We’ve doubled and tripled that team since then. We’ve already made the investment. Historically we’ve moved upmarket and we’ve gone after the enterprise, but we understand that there’s a path for both. The reality is for us to continue growing at the pace that we’re growing at right now, the midmarket has to be a part of our business.”

ServiceNow launches conversational interface to its service desk
ServiceNow Inc. is enhancing the artificial intelligence features in its service desk offering with Flow, a feature that handles employee requests via a natural language interface with extensive automation.
The company said it’s targeting organizations that want to automate support without undertaking a full information technology service management implementation.
The product lets employees seek help through Slack and Microsoft Teams, receive answers drawn from company information and complete routine requests within those conversations. ServiceNow said teams can get Flow running in a day without an implementation project or additional infrastructure.
Built on an entirely new technology stack, Flow gives ServiceNow an entry point for companies that have avoided buying ITSM software because of its complexity. It also targets departments, remote offices and newly acquired business units within enterprises that already use ServiceNow.
The launch broadens ServiceNow’s reach to buyers seeking a service desk they can activate directly, while keeping connections to its enterprise software portfolio.
“Flow is for companies that want to work in a completely new way,” said Jeff Hausman, executive vice president and general manager of technology workflow products at ServiceNow. “It’s automation built for speed and simplicity.”
The service is designed around recurring requests such as password resets, account unlocks, access provisioning, policy questions and basic troubleshooting. Employees describe their problems in natural language, and Flow retrieves relevant information and acts or escalates the request to a support team with the conversation’s context.
Once a support worker resolves an issue, an IT manager can turn that solution into an automated workflow with a single click, ServiceNow said. Subsequent requests can then be handled automatically, without requiring a developer or a newly written knowledge base article.
That approach extends the product beyond answering questions: ServiceNow said Flow can close requests or route them to the right people when needed. More than 100 prebuilt connectors link the service to systems containing knowledge, assets and ticketing information or supporting automated actions.
A demonstration showed an employee asking about company holidays in Slack and receiving an answer linked to a source document. When the employee subsequently reports trouble accessing a human resources system, Flow offers to open a ServiceNow incident and collects details about the problem.
The demonstration also shows an automation that sends virtual private network guidance, checks whether access has been restored, determines whether approval is necessary and requests a manager’s authorization before proceeding. Another workflow illustrates employee onboarding, including joining a workspace and provisioning access credentials.
For enterprises, Flor is intended to give smaller teams a faster way to deploy support while retaining access to the company’s wider service management environment. ServiceNow also plans to extend the conversational model beyond IT into areas including customer support and procurement.
“The real value comes when those solutions can be easily automated and repeated at scale,” said Stephen Elliot, group vice president of software development and IT operations at International Data Corp., as quoted in a ServiceNow press release.
Customers cited in the announcement described applications beyond traditional internal IT support. One said it uses shared Slack channels to support clients, while two software companies pointed to simpler proesses for retrieving internal knowledge and reducing repeated questions.
“Someone asks a question in Slack, Flow pulls answers from what we’ve already documented, and if it’s something new, we escalate it and learn from it, and Flow automates it the next time,” said Mitch Stutler, co-founder and chief executive of ServiceNow partner VividCharts Inc.
Flow is available now. Pricing is consumption-based, with a free trial offered before purchase. Existing ServiceNow customers with AI entitlements will draw from their current pool of assists without buying an additional product license. ServiceNow did not disclose specific consumption rates. New customers will be able to purchase Flow with a credit card without an existing ServiceNow relationship.

ServiceNow (NOW) shares have significantly lagged the broader market over the past year. The stock has declined 27%, while the S&P 500 Index ($SPX) has gained approximately 15.3% over the same period.
Several factors have contributed to the weakness. Investors are increasingly concerned that more capable generative artificial intelligence (AI) models could displace software-as-a-service (SaaS) applications, putting pressure on software stocks such as ServiceNow. Geopolitical tensions and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have also delayed some subscription agreements, creating near-term headwinds for the company.

However, these near-term challenges do not appear to have undermined ServiceNow's underlying business momentum. The company continues to deliver solid growth. At the same time, its key performance metrics remain encouraging.
Rather than being displaced by AI, ServiceNow is positioning the technology as a growth catalyst. Its expanding AI capabilities are accelerating its growth, deepening customer relationships, and creating additional opportunities for long-term growth.
An expanding customer base, larger deal sizes, more customers adopting multiple products, and accelerating uptake of AI-powered solutions indicate that demand for ServiceNow's platform remains robust.
Thanks to the solid demand, its subscription business continues to grow at a solid pace. ServiceNow's subscription revenue reached $3.98 billion in Q2, increasing 23% year-over-year (YoY). Remaining performance obligations (RPO) rose 22% to $29 billion, with longer contract durations providing greater predictability in future subscription growth.
Demand was broad-based across ServiceNow's workflow portfolio. IT Service Management (ITSM) was featured in 15 of the company's 20 largest deals, while IT Operations Management (ITOM) appeared in 18. Security and risk solutions were included in 16 of the top 20 deals, alongside strong demand for CRM, industry, core business, and creative workflows. This product breadth indicates that customers are increasingly consolidating workflows on ServiceNow, potentially increasing platform dependency and creating additional expansion opportunities.
Customer retention and expansion provide another structural growth driver. ServiceNow's renewal rate was 98% in Q2, underscoring the durability of its installed base. By the end of the quarter, the company had 658 customers with annual contract value (ACV) exceeding $5 million. Meanwhile, 32 additional customers crossed the $20 million threshold over the past year. Moreover, 18 of the top 20 deals included at least eight products, suggesting that larger customers are steadily increasing their platform penetration.
AI is becoming an increasingly material growth catalyst. ServiceNow AI ACV exceeded $1 billion, with net new AI ACV rising more than 40% sequentially. Deals involving at least five AI products increased 5.5x YoY, while customers running agentic AI in production rose ninefold over nine months. First-time buyers of ServiceNow's agentic AI offerings also increased more than 45% YoY.
ServiceNow reported that new AI-native products are generating price increases consistent with the company's targeted 20%-30% framework. Moreover, the company is already tracking ahead of its objective for AI to represent 30% of ACV by 2030. Overall, recurring revenue visibility, deeper platform adoption, and accelerating AI monetization create multiple avenues for ServiceNow to sustain growth.
ServiceNow's underlying fundamentals remain strong. Although concerns about AI disruption and delays in near-term deal activity have weighed on the stock, several key indicators continue to point to durable demand. Accelerating AI adoption, strong customer retention, larger deal sizes, and robust RPO growth all support the company's long-term outlook.
More importantly, ServiceNow is using AI as a growth catalyst, expanding monetization opportunities, increasing customer engagement, and creating new avenues for revenue growth.
Thanks to strong demand, ServiceNow raised its 2026 subscription revenue outlook by $15 million at the midpoint to $15.76 billion-$15.77 billion, representing 21% YoY growth.
Analysts are bullish and maintain a "Strong Buy" consensus rating on NOW stock.
With strong momentum in subscription revenue, visibility into future growth, and AI emerging as an increasingly important growth driver, ServiceNow stock has strong upside potential.

Diana David calls herself a "forward-deployed futurist." She says CEOs kept asking for "forward-deployed" employees, "people to be out on the edge, to bring us back the insights about what is actually happening in AI in our companies."
What she is finding is that the companies pulling ahead on AI are not distinguished mainly by their technology. At the Fortune AIQ Summit on Thursday, David, who also serves as ServiceNow's director of futures, said the widest gaps between the leaders and everyone else are about people.

By David's account, 64% are on a path to unified data, versus 14%. And around 57% have "a clear, strong AI vision," versus 21%.
Then there are the autonomous workflows. About 59% of companies surveyed are past the pilot phase, David said. "Only 9% are doing agentic, autonomous, multistep workflows that are not checked by human beings at every step." Among pacesetters the share is 36%, against 2% of others. These workflows are "not just one little point of sale," she said.
That distinction drives what David called her "pet peeve": "AI adoption for everyone."
"I get it, because it's a great CEO story," she said. "95% of everybody has X, Y, Z. But it is not translating into productivity, and it's often not with training, and that doesn't equal maturity."
Kahn had set up the problem. Many companies gave employees AI tools and "let a thousand flowers bloom," he said. Then they decided it was too expensive, with no productivity gain. Now they are narrowing to specific use cases. Kahn also pointed to companies that dropped agents into existing workflows, or swapped an employee for one.
David said the answer starts higher up. "I think it starts with leadership," she said. "Growth mindset, an idea, and a vision for change of what the company can become, followed with specific training around AI and specific functions."
She urged executives to think "almost in a day zero mentality" about what process would be designed from scratch. The alternative, she said, is to "sprinkle AI on something, probably a very old or broken process, to make it go even faster. That's just not solving the problem faster."
Kahn pressed on a worry he said executives voice: The technology moves so fast that a redesigned process may be obsolete next year. David said she hears that, too. Her answer was to have a vision, align the data, choose workflows, assign ownership, and "iterate … I don't think that any company is going to succeed by doing some kind of top-down plan where one person or one strategy team is redesigning everything immediately," she said.
She pointed to ServiceNow's AI Control Tower as one way to see across the organization. "You have to have transparency," she said. "Having the visibility from across the organization and a very strong foundation allows you to be flexible."
Most companies are behind on the human side. According to the report, 59% of organizations lack long-term HR plans for AI, and 42% of employees say they aren't getting enough AI training. The report puts pacesetters' average ROI at 160%.

"It is everything, everywhere, all at once," David said.
The index itself has been volatile. "In 2024 we started this, and we thought, 'It's just going to go up and up and up,'" David said. Then the average score fell from 44 to 35. She added that ServiceNow plans to add agentic AI to the AIQ next year, and the measure will turn on "what are we deploying and where," and whether companies are "realizing actual commercial value." That, she said, "is what I think true maturity for business is going to mean, versus everybody has, you know, AI in their pocket."
